newsitem.title: USA: Brisk US soy movement may reflect river re-opening.
newsitem.headline: Brisk US soy movement may reflect river re-opening.

text.p: Greater-than-expected weekly soybean export inspections reported Monday may partially reflect an easing of backlogged shipments along the Mississippi River rather than a dramatic surge in export business, exporters said.
"You have to be a little cautious just looking at pure numbers. Maybe, this bigger number could be an accumulation of the last three or four weeks of delays," one exporter said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture on Monday reported weekly soybean export inspections at 18.9 million bushels, above trade expectations of nine million to 13 million.
The figure was also well above the previous week's figure of 8.9 million bushels.
The exporter said in order to determine if shipments are actually higher, a pattern of three to four weeks of comparable numbers would be needed.

The data sparked a bump up in the May and July old-crop soybean contracts on the Chicago Board of Trade, with May ending 1/2 cent a bushel higher at $8.68-1/4 a bushel after surging as high as $8.77. July ended down two cents at $8.65. In contrast, new-crop contracts all ended several cents lower.
"We might come in next week with five million bushels and average it out to where it is supposed to be," the exporter said.
A second exporter said high water on the Mississippi slowed barges for several weeks. "We were kind of overdue for a big export week," he said, referring to an easing of delays.

However, several locks along the upper Mississippi River re-opened to navigation over the weekend as high water levels fed by melted snow, slowly fell from St Anthony Falls, Minn., to Dubuque, Iowa, the U.S. Coast Guard said on Monday.
"I don't see any reason to get all cooked up on the weekly export inspections," the second exporter said. "They just tell us of business that is already on the books."
He added weekly export sales were a better indicator.
"We still have a pretty good chunk of sales that we need to execute sooner or later," he said.
But if export inspections continue to come in strong, something has to give -- either an increase in soybean supplies or decrease in demand, exporters noted.
U.S. soybean ending stocks for 1996/97 were forecast to be the lowest in 20 years with the USDA expecting stocks of 125 million bushels remaining on September 1.
"We either have to reduce our crush dramatically over the next month or import beans," a third exporter said.
Some U.S. firms have already imported Brazilian soybeans this spring because Brazilian pricers were lower and said to be more profitable.
In the week ended April 23, crushers processed 25.6 million bushels, slightly down from the prior week of 26.20 million, the National Oilseed Processors Association said.

Earlier Monday, a South America-based Sparks Companies official said the U.S. might have to import "a significant quantity" of soybeans if current trends continue. Sparks is a Memphis, Tenn.-based agricultural consultant firm.
